title: Fast Walkers See Slower Cognitive Decline
paragraphs: Older adults who walk quickly may be much less likely to experience a decline in their memory and thinking skills, according to a new study from the United States.

The study was published in the medical journal Neurology in July 2026. Its authors included Dr. Sofiya Milman of Albert Einstein College of Medicine and Dr. Joe Verghese of Stony Brook Medicine. The researchers analyzed data from nearly 4,000 older adults who were taking part in a long-term study on aging.

The participants took a timed walking test to measure how fast they walked. The researchers then identified a group they called "super movers." These were people over the age of 80 whose walking speed was much faster than that of other people their age. They made up the fastest 9% of the participants.
The results were striking. According to Milman, super movers were about 50% less likely to develop cognitive decline than people who were not super movers.

The researchers also found that super movers tended to keep the size of their hippocampus as they got older. The hippocampus is a part of the brain that is important for memory and finding your way around. Interestingly, some super movers had plaques and tangles in their brains, which are linked to Alzheimer's disease, but they did not show any symptoms. The researchers suggest that movement may help the brain stay resilient despite these changes.

However, the researchers were careful not to claim that walking fast directly protects the brain. According to Verghese, fast walking is a sign that the brain and body are aging well. Genetics may also play a role in who becomes a super mover.

Still, the experts believe that staying active is important. Verghese's advice is simple: keep moving. The researchers say that the type of activity, such as walking, swimming or cycling, matters less than doing it regularly.
Other research has also suggested that healthy habits, such as eating well, sleeping well and staying socially connected, can help protect the brain.
